```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
# pcaMethods is loaded first on purpose: it masks a few base/stats functions,
# and loading the tidyverse packages afterwards restores the ones we need.
library(pcaMethods)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
library(knitr)
library(DT)
library(tidyr)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ComplexHeatmap))
# circlize provides colorRamp2() for the heatmap colour scale
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(circlize))

# Set up tutorial options
tutorial_options(exercise.timelimit = 60)

# load the data
food_data <- read.csv(
  file = "./foods.csv",
  header = TRUE
)

# Store variable names for easy reference
food_vars <- names(food_data)[5:ncol(food_data)]
n_vars <- length(food_vars)

# The food variables as a plain matrix, which is what pcaMethods expects
food_matrix <- as.matrix(food_data[, food_vars])
rownames(food_matrix) <- food_data$Country

# Colours and labels for the geographic regions, used in several plots
region_colors <- c("C" = "#E69F00", "S" = "#D55E00", "N" = "#0072B2",
                   "U" = "#009E73", "X" = "#CC79A7")
region_labels <- c("C" = "Central", "S" = "Southern", "N" = "Northern",
                   "U" = "UK/Ireland", "X" = "Benelux")
```

```{r prep-pca}
# Setup chunk: makes the PCA model available to the exercises below.
# learnr runs each exercise in its own environment, so anything an exercise
# needs has to come from the global setup chunk or from a setup chunk like
# this one, referenced with the exercise.setup chunk option.
# (Note: a setup chunk must NOT be named "<something>-setup" unless an
# exercise with that exact name exists, so we use the "prep-" prefix.)
pca_food <- pcaMethods::pca(food_matrix,
                            method = "nipals",
                            nPcs = 5,
                            scale = "uv",     # unit variance, i.e. UV scaling
                            center = TRUE)

r2_values <- pca_food@R2
r2_cumulative <- R2cum(pca_food)

food_scores   <- scores(pca_food)
food_loadings <- loadings(pca_food)
```

```{r prep-scores, exercise.setup="prep-pca"}
scores_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[, 1],
  PC2 = food_scores[, 2],
  PC3 = food_scores[, 3],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Geographic_Location = food_data$Geographic_Location,
  Capitol_Latitude = food_data$Capitol_Latitude
)
```

## How to use this tutorial

This works exactly like the IRIS tutorial, so if you have just finished that one
you can go straight to the next section.

The grey boxes are live R code: press **Run Code** to execute a box, 
**Start Over** to restore the original code, and **Solution** (where it is 
offered) to see one possible answer. You are encouraged to change the code and 
run it again.

Answer the questions with **Submit Answer** and read the explanation that
follows - it is usually the most useful part, also when you were right. Sections
appear one at a time; press **Continue** to move on, and your progress is
remembered if you close the page.

Remember that each code box runs independently: an object created in one box is
not automatically available in the next.

## Background

Data were collected to investigate the consumption pattern of a number of provisions in different European countries. The purpose of the investigation was to examine similarities and differences between the countries and the possible explanations.

### Objective

In this tutorial you will:

- Explain why there are groupings in multivariate plots
- Identify data characteristics that differentiate Portugal and Spain from Sweden and Denmark
- Understand geographic and cultural patterns in food consumption across Europe
- Practice interpreting PCA results with real-world data

### The Data

The dataset consists of **20 variables** (different foods) and **16 observations** (European countries). The values are the percentages of households in each country where a particular product was found.

Let's explore the data structure:

```{r explore-data, exercise=TRUE}
# Display the data
datatable(food_data,
          options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
          caption = "European Food Consumption Data")

# Get summary statistics for the food variables
summary(food_data[, food_vars])
```

```{r explore-data-solution}
head(food_data, 10)
summary(food_data[, food_vars])
```

A few values are missing (you will spot them as `NA` in the summary above), but
the NIPALS algorithm we use below handles them directly, so there is nothing you
need to do about them.

### Data Exploration

It's always good to have a closer look at the data structure. Which columns are 
numbers and which columns are characters or categories.

```{r data-structure, exercise=TRUE}
# Check the structure
str(food_data)

# Count countries by geographic location
table(food_data$Geographic_Location)

# Geographic locations:
# C = Central, S = Southern, N = Northern, U = UK/Ireland, X = Benelux
```

<div id="data-structure-hint">
**Hint:** The `Geographic_Location` variable groups the countries:
C = Central Europe, S = Southern Europe, N = Northern Europe,
U = UK/Ireland, X = Benelux.
</div>

## Principal Component Analysis

### Performing PCA

We use the `pca()` function from the **pcaMethods** package, with the **NIPALS**
algorithm. `scale = "uv"` applies unit variance scaling, so that every food 
counts equally regardless of how common it is.

```{r pca-basic, exercise=TRUE}
# food_matrix holds the 20 food variables, with the countries as row names
pca_food <- pcaMethods::pca(food_matrix,
                            method = "nipals",
                            nPcs = 5,
                            scale = "uv",     # unit variance scaling
                            center = TRUE)

# Display the summary
summary(pca_food)

# The scores and loadings are pulled out with their own accessor functions
food_scores   <- scores(pca_food)     # 16 countries x 5 components
food_loadings <- loadings(pca_food)   # 20 foods    x 5 components
```

```{r pca-basic-solution}
pca_food <- pcaMethods::pca(food_matrix, method = "nipals", nPcs = 5,
                            scale = "uv", center = TRUE)
summary(pca_food)

food_scores   <- scores(pca_food)
food_loadings <- loadings(pca_food)
```

### Model quality: R² and Q²

By default only the **R²** is calculated. On its own it is not enough to judge 
a model, because R² can only ever increase when you add a component.
**Q²cum** is the cross-validated counterpart: the observations are split into 7
groups, each group is left out in turn, and the model built on the rest is used
to predict it. Q² therefore measures how much the model can *predict*, not just
describe - and unlike R², it can go **down** when a component starts fitting
noise.

```{r r2-q2, exercise=TRUE}
set.seed(2026)  # cross-validation splits the data randomly

pca_cv <- pcaMethods::pca(food_matrix, method = "nipals", nPcs = 5,
                          scale = "uv", center = TRUE)

r2cum <- R2cum(pca_cv)
q2cum <- Q2(pca_cv, food_matrix, fold = 7, verbose = FALSE)

data.frame(
  Component = paste0("PC", seq_along(r2cum)),
  R2cum = round(r2cum, 3),
  Q2cum = round(q2cum[seq_along(r2cum)], 3)
)
```

Look carefully at the two columns. R²cum climbs steadily, but Q²cum peaks
around the third component and then falls away.

Note that with only 16 countries the cross-validation is noisy, so your Q²
values will shift a little every time the random split changes. The *pattern* -
low values throughout, peaking at 3 components - is stable; the exact numbers
are not.

### Quiz: Model Quality

```{r quiz-pca-quality, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("Based on the PCA summary, how many principal components would you consider sufficient to describe the data?",
    answer("1 component"),
    answer("2 components"),
    answer("3 components", correct = TRUE),
    answer("All 20 components"),
    message = "PC1 explains 31.6% and PC2 19.2%, so the first two components together reach only 50.9%. PC3 adds another 13.8%, bringing the total to 64.7%. That is why we will also look at PC1 vs PC3 later in this tutorial: PC3 still contains real structure."
  ),
  question("What can you say about the quality of this PCA model compared to the IRIS dataset?",
    answer("Much better - higher R²"),
    answer("About the same"),
    answer("Not as good - lower R²", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Cannot compare different datasets"),
    message = "For IRIS, two components already covered 95.8% of the variance; here two components reach only 50.9%. Food consumption data is more complex and variable than flower measurements, so we expect lower R² values. This is normal for behavioural/social data."
  ),
  question("Q²cum for this model never rises above about 0.2, and starts dropping after the third component. What does that mean?",
    answer("The model describes some real structure, but its predictive ability is poor", correct = TRUE),
    answer("The model is excellent, because Q² is positive"),
    answer("The model is broken and the results cannot be interpreted at all"),
    answer("Q² is irrelevant for PCA"),
    message = "Compare this with IRIS, where Q²cum reached 0.71. A Q² of around 0.15 means the model captures a genuine but weak pattern: you can use it to explore and to generate hypotheses about which countries resemble each other, but you should not expect it to predict a new country's shopping basket. The fact that Q² falls after the third component is the signal to stop adding components - the fourth and fifth are fitting noise.",
    correct = "Correct - and note that R² alone would never have told you this. R² keeps climbing all the way to component 5."
  )
)
```

## Scores Plot (PC1 vs PC2)

The scores plot shows how countries are positioned based on their food consumption patterns:

```{r scores-plot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Prepare scores data
scores_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[,1],
  PC2 = food_scores[,2],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Geographic_Location = food_data$Geographic_Location,
  Capitol_Latitude = food_data$Capitol_Latitude
)

# Create scores plot colored by geographic location
p <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, 
                           color = Geographic_Location, label = Country)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.7, hjust = 0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "PCA Scores Plot - European Food Consumption",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(r2_values[1]*100, 1), "% variance)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(r2_values[2]*100, 1), "% variance)"),
       color = "Region") +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors,
                     labels = region_labels) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(p, tooltips = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))
```

```{r scores-plot-solution}
scores_df <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[,1],
  PC2 = food_scores[,2],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Geographic_Location = food_data$Geographic_Location
)

p <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, 
                           color = Geographic_Location, label = Country)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.7, hjust = 0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "PCA Scores Plot - European Food Consumption",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(r2_values[1]*100, 1), "% variance)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", round(r2_values[2]*100, 1), "% variance)"),
       color = "Region") +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors,
                     labels = region_labels) +

ggplotly(p, tooltips = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))
```

### Quiz: Identifying Clusters

```{r quiz-clusters, echo=FALSE}
quiz(

    answer("No clusters"),
    answer("Yes, some regional patterns", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Perfect separation by region"),
    answer("Only 2 distinct clusters"),
    message = "Colouring by geographic location reveals roughly three groups: the Northern countries (Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Finland), the Southern countries (Portugal, Italy, Spain, and Austria alongside them), and the rest. The groups overlap, so this is a tendency rather than a clean separation."
  ),

    answer("Portugal and England", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Portugal and Sweden"),
    answer("Germany and France"),
    answer("Norway and Denmark"),
    message = "Portugal sits at the far negative end of PC1 (-4.6) and England at the far positive end (+3.9), which makes them the two countries furthest apart. ## Outliers: Hotelling's T² and DModX
```

Before interpreting the loadings, check whether any single country is distorting
the model. **Hotelling's T²** finds strong outliers lying far from the centre
*within* the model plane, drawn as a confidence ellipse on the scores plot.
**DModX** finds observations lying far *away* from the plane, which a scores
plot cannot show you at all.

```{r outliers, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-scores", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
n <- nrow(scores_df)
A <- 2
sd_pc <- apply(food_scores[, 1:A], 2, sd)

scores_df$T2 <- rowSums((food_scores[, 1:A] / rep(sd_pc, each = n))^2)
t2_crit <- (A * (n - 1) * (n + 1)) / (n * (n - A)) * qf(0.95, A, n - A)

theta <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 200)
ellipse <- data.frame(
  PC1 = sd_pc[1] * sqrt(t2_crit) * cos(theta),
  PC2 = sd_pc[2] * sqrt(t2_crit) * sin(theta)
)

p <- ggplot(scores_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_path(data = ellipse, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Geographic_Location), size = 4, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Country), vjust = -0.9, size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors, labels = region_labels) +
  labs(title = "Scores plot with 95% Hotelling's T² ellipse",
       colour = "Region") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(p, tooltips = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))

outside <- scores_df$Country[scores_df$T2 > t2_crit]
cat("Critical value (95%):", round(t2_crit, 2), "\n")
cat("Countries outside the ellipse:",
    if (length(outside) == 0) "none" else paste(outside, collapse = ", "), "\n")

# The two most extreme countries, even though they stay inside:
head(scores_df[order(-scores_df$T2), c("Country", "T2")], 3)
```

Nothing falls outside the ellipse. That is worth pausing on: Sweden
(T² = 6.1) is the most extreme country, followed by Portugal (3.6) and
England (3.3), yet with only 16 observations the 95% ellipse is so wide that
none of them crosses it. A small data 
set has very little power to flag outliers, so the absence of a flag is not 
evidence that everything is fine.

```{r dmodx, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# completeObs() returns the data matrix with the few missing cells filled in by
# the model itself, which is what DModX needs to compute a residual per country.
dmodx_df <- data.frame(
  Country = food_data$Country,
  DModX = as.numeric(DModX(pca_food, completeObs(pca_food)))
)

p <- ggplot(dmodx_df, aes(x = reorder(Country, DModX), y = DModX)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dotted", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "DModX (normalised)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

ggplotly(p, tooltips = c("text", "colour", "x", "y")) |>
  layout(
    title = list(
      text = paste0(
        "DModX per observation",
        "<br>",
        "<sup>Dashed = model average (1), red dotted = rule-of-thumb limit (2)</sup>"
      ),
      x = 0,
      y = 1,
      xanchor = "left",
      yanchor = "top",
      xref = "paper",
      yref = "paper"
    )
  )
```

### Quiz: Outlier diagnostics

```{r quiz-outliers, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("Based on the T² ellipse and the DModX plot, are there countries you should remove?",
    answer("No - nothing is extreme enough to justify removal", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Yes, Sweden and Portugal, because they are the most extreme"),
    answer("Yes, all Northern European countries"),
    answer("Yes, the countries with missing values"),
    message = "No country falls outside the 95% T² ellipse, and the highest DModX (France, 1.4) does not come close to twice the model average. Sweden has the highest T2 value, but this is  precisely because their diets differ most, which is the pattern we are trying to study. Removing observations with a large / extreme T2 value would delete the very signal you are after. Outlier diagnostics exist to make you go and LOOK at a sample, not to delete it automatically."
  ),
  question("Why is DModX worth looking at when you already have the scores plot?",
    answer("DModX is just another way of drawing the scores plot"),
    answer("DModX replaces the need for R² and Q²"),
    answer("DModX measures how important each food item is"),
    answer("A country can sit comfortably inside the ellipse and still be poorly described by the model", correct = TRUE),
    message = "The scores plot only shows you the part of an observation that the model DOES capture. DModX measures the residual - the part it misses. An observation can look perfectly ordinary in the scores plot and still have a large DModX."
  )
)
```

## Loadings Plot

<div class="alert alert-info">
**A word of warning about signs.** The direction of a principal component is
arbitrary: a component and its mirror image describe exactly the same model. Your
plot may therefore be flipped compared with a fellow student's screen, and the 
sign of a loading on its own means nothing.

What *is* meaningful is the relative arrangement: which foods sit together,
which sit on opposite sides of the origin, and how far each lies from the
centre. Always read a loadings plot together with its scores plot - foods in one
corner of the loadings plot are the ones consumed most in the countries sitting
in that same corner of the scores plot.
</div>

The loadings plot shows which food items contribute most to the patterns we see:

```{r loadings-plot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Prepare loadings data
loadings_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(food_loadings),
  PC1 = food_loadings[,1],
  PC2 = food_loadings[,2]
)

# Create loadings plot
p <- ggplot(loadings_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Variable), 
            vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0.5, 
            size = 2.5, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, 
             colour = "grey") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
             colour = "grey") +
  labs(title = "PCA Loadings Plot",
       x = "PC1 Loadings",
       y = "PC2 Loadings") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(p, tooltips = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))
```

### Biplot: scores and loadings in one plot

A **biplot** puts the countries (points) and the foods (arrows) on the same
axes, so you can read the two together instead of flipping between plots. A
country lies in the direction of the foods its households buy most, and the
longer an arrow, the more that food drives the picture. Foods whose arrows
point the same way tend to be found together.

This is the quickest way to answer the question that follows.

```{r biplot, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Scores and loadings in one picture. The loadings are much smaller numbers than
# the scores, so they are multiplied by a constant to make both fill the same
# axes. Only the DIRECTION and the relative length of an arrow carry meaning,
# never its absolute size - try changing arrow_scale and you will see the arrows
# grow while the picture stays the same.
arrow_scale <- 8

biplot_scores <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[, 1],
  PC2 = food_scores[, 2],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Region = food_data$Geographic_Location
)

biplot_loadings <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_loadings[, 1] * arrow_scale,
  PC2 = food_loadings[, 2] * arrow_scale,
  Food = rownames(food_loadings)
)

ggplot(biplot_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_segment(data = biplot_loadings,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm")), colour = "grey45") +
  geom_text(data = biplot_loadings, aes(label = Food),
            size = 2.5, colour = "grey25", vjust = -0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Region), size = 4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Country), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = region_colors, labels = region_labels) +
  labs(title = "PCA biplot - food consumption patterns",
       subtitle = "countries = points, foods = arrows") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Identify Top Contributing Variables

```{r top-loadings, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca"}
# Find variables with strongest loadings on PC1
pc1_loadings <- sort(abs(food_loadings[,1]), decreasing = TRUE)
cat("Top 5 variables contributing to PC1:\n")
print(head(pc1_loadings, 5))

# Find variables with strongest loadings on PC2
pc2_loadings <- sort(abs(food_loadings[,2]), decreasing = TRUE)
cat("\nTop 5 variables contributing to PC2:\n")
print(head(pc2_loadings, 5))

# Show actual direction (positive or negative)
cat("\nPC1 loadings (with direction):\n")
print(sort(food_loadings[,1], decreasing = TRUE)[1:5])
cat("\nPC1 loadings (negative direction):\n")
print(sort(food_loadings[,1], decreasing = FALSE)[1:5])
```

### Quiz: Interpreting Loadings

```{r quiz-loadings, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("Portugal and England are the two countries furthest apart in the scores plot. Which foods are the main cause of this separation?",
    answer("Tinned fruit and tinned soup: England buys them a lot, Portugal hardly at all", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Garlic and olive oil"),
    answer("Crisp bread and frozen fish"),
    answer("Butter and margarine"),
    message = "Portugal and England sit at opposite ends of PC1. Garlic and olive oil are the obvious guess, because they mark the Mediterranean side of PC1 - but England's olive oil consumption (57%) is actually about average, and garlic explains only a small part of the gap. The bigger difference lies at the other end of PC1. Tinned fruit (England 89%, Portugal 8%) and tinned soup (76% against 1%) contribute most, followed by jam, biscuits, apples and instant coffee - all much more common in England. So the separation is mainly 'England buys a lot of tinned and processed food', not 'Portugal uses a lot of garlic'. Always check the raw data before settling on the most obvious explanation."
  ),
  question("The Northern countries (Sweden, Denmark, Norway and Finland) sit at the top of the scores plot. What makes them different from the rest of Europe?",
    answer("A high consumption of crisp bread, frozen fish and frozen vegetables", correct = TRUE),
    answer("A high consumption of garlic and olive oil"),
    answer("A high consumption of tinned soup and instant coffee"),
    answer("Nothing - they sit in the middle of the scores plot"),
    message = "The Northern countries lie on the positive side of PC2, and the foods with the largest positive PC2 loadings are crisp bread (0.39), frozen fish (0.37) and frozen vegetables (0.27). The raw data agree: crisp bread is found in 63% of Nordic households against 16% elsewhere, frozen fish in 38% against 16%, and frozen vegetables in 28% against 12%. The other end of PC2 tells the same story from the opposite side: instant coffee has the most negative PC2 loading (-0.41), and the Nordic countries use much less of it (15% against 47%)."
  )
)
```

## PC1 vs PC3 Analysis

Let's examine PC1 vs PC3 to understand other patterns:

```{r scores-pc1-pc3, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Prepare scores data for PC1 vs PC3
scores_df_pc3 <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[,1],
  PC3 = food_scores[,3],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Geographic_Location = food_data$Geographic_Location
)

# Create scores plot
p <- ggplot(scores_df_pc3, aes(x = PC1, y = PC3, 
                          color = Geographic_Location, label = Country)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.7, hjust = 0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "PCA Scores Plot - PC1 vs PC3",
       x = paste0("PC1 (", round(r2_values[1]*100, 1), "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC3 (", round(r2_values[3]*100, 1), "%)"),
       color = "Region") +
  scale_color_manual(values = region_colors,
                     labels = region_labels) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))
```

### PC3 Loadings

```{r loadings-pc3, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Examine PC3 loadings
loadings_pc3 <- data.frame(
  Variable = rownames(food_loadings),
  PC1 = food_loadings[,1],
  PC3 = food_loadings[,3]
)

p <- ggplot(loadings_pc3, aes(x = PC1, y = PC3)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Variable), 
            vjust = -0.5, hjust = 0.5, 
            size = 2.5, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "PCA Loadings Plot - PC1 vs PC3",
       x = "PC1 Loadings",
       y = "PC3 Loadings") +
  theme_minimal() 

ggplotly(p, tooltip = c("text", "colour", "x", "y"))

# Show top contributors to PC3
cat("\nTop contributors to PC3:\n")
print(sort(abs(food_loadings[,3]), decreasing = TRUE)[1:5])
```

#### Biplot: scores and loadings in one plot

A **biplot** puts the countries (points) and the foods (arrows) on the same
axes, so you can read the two together instead of flipping between plots. A
country lies in the direction of the foods its households buy most, and the
longer an arrow, the more that food drives the picture. Foods whose arrows
point the same way tend to be found together.

```{r biplot2, exercise=TRUE, exercise.setup="prep-pca", fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
# Scores and loadings in one picture. The loadings are much smaller numbers than
# the scores, so they are multiplied by a constant to make both fill the same
# axes. Only the DIRECTION and the relative length of an arrow carry meaning,
# never its absolute size - try changing arrow_scale and you will see the arrows
# grow while the picture stays the same.
arrow_scale <- 8

biplot_scores <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_scores[, 1],
  PC3 = food_scores[, 3],
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Region = food_data$Geographic_Location
)

biplot_loadings <- data.frame(
  PC1 = food_loadings[, 1] * arrow_scale,
  PC3 = food_loadings[, 3] * arrow_scale,
  Food = rownames(food_loadings)
)

ggplot(biplot_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC3)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey") +
  geom_segment(data = biplot_loadings,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC3),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm")), colour = "grey45") +
  geom_text(data = biplot_loadings, aes(label = Food),
            size = 2.5, colour = "grey25", vjust = -0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Region), size = 4, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Country), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = region_colors, labels = region_labels) +
  labs(title = "PCA biplot - food consumption patterns",
       subtitle = "countries = points, foods = arrows") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

#### One food at a time

A biplot shows the overall picture, but it is always worth checking the raw
data behind it. The plot below shows, for one food, the percentage of
households in each country where it was found. Change `food` to any of the
other food names (listed at the top of the output) and press **Run Code**
again. Which foods really set England and Ireland apart?

```{r food-per-country, exercise=TRUE, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
# The available foods
food_vars

# Pick a food (copy one of the names below)
food <- "Ground_Coffee"

plot_df <- data.frame(
  Country = food_data$Country,
  Region  = food_data$Geographic_Location,
  Value   = food_data[[food]]
)

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = reorder(Country, Value), y = Value, fill = Region)) +
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # dashed line = the European average for this food
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(plot_df$Value, na.rm = TRUE),
             linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors, labels = region_labels) +
  labs(title = paste("Households with", food, "per country"),
       subtitle = "dashed line = European average",
       x = NULL, y = "% of households") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

### Quiz: PC1 vs PC3 Interpretation

```{r quiz-pc3, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("England and Ireland are separated from the rest of Europe along PC3. Which variable contributes most to this separation?",
    answer("Their unusually LOW consumption of ground coffee", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Their high tea consumption"),
    answer("Their high tinned soup consumption"),
    answer("Their high yoghurt consumption"),
    message = "This one is worth looking at carefully. At first glance jam, tea and tinned soup seem to be the obvious explanation, but check the loadings: ground coffee has by far the largest PC3 loading (0.48). England (27%) and Ireland (30%) are far below every other country - the next lowest is Austria at 55%. Tea does not actually discriminate: England and Ireland are at 99%, but Holland (98%), Sweden (93%) and Denmark (92%) are just as high. Tinned soup does not either: England is at 76% but Ireland at 18%, which is exactly the European average. Jam does contribute (loading -0.30, both around 90% against a mean of 55%), just less than ground coffee."
  ),
  question("How does the Garlic and Olive oil intake of England/Ireland compare to the rest of Europe?",
    answer("Garlic much lower, olive oil about average", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Both much lower than average"),
    answer("Both much higher than average"),
    answer("Garlic about average, olive oil much lower"),
    message = "Garlic: Ireland (5%) is the lowest of all 16 countries and England (11%) is among the lowest, against a European mean of 42%. Olive oil is a different story: England is at 57% and Ireland at 31%, against a mean of 54% - so England is even slightly above average. Compare that with Spain (86% garlic, 91% olive oil) or Italy (80% and 94%). It is a useful reminder to check the actual variable plots instead of assuming that two variables which sit close together in one loadings plot always behave the same way."
  )
)
```

## Hierarchical clustering: a second unsupervised view

PCA is not the only unsupervised way to look for groups. **Hierarchical
clustering** joins the countries that are most alike, step by step, into a
tree (a dendrogram). Like PCA, it never sees the regions.

In the heatmap below, each column is scaled to a **z-score**, so the colour says
how far a country lies above (red) or below (blue) the European average *for
that food* - the same unit variance scaling the PCA used. Both countries and foods are reordered by
hierarchical clustering, and the coloured bar on the right shows the geographic
region, which is **not** used by the clustering.

```{r univariate-viz, exercise=TRUE, fig.width=8, fig.height=6.5}
# Scale each food to a z-score so the 20 foods are on a comparable footing
food_z <- scale(food_matrix)

# Geographic region as an annotation bar next to the rows
region_annotation <- rowAnnotation(
  Region = food_data$Geographic_Location,
  col = list(Region = region_colors),
  annotation_legend_param = list(
    Region = list(at = names(region_labels), labels = region_labels)
  )
)

Heatmap(
  food_z,
  name = "z-score",
  col = colorRamp2(c(-2, 0, 2), c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B")),
  right_annotation = region_annotation,
  # hierarchical clustering on both countries and foods.
  # dist() simply skips the few missing cells, so nothing needs imputing.
  clustering_distance_rows    = "euclidean",
  clustering_method_rows      = "ward.D2",
  clustering_distance_columns = "euclidean",
  clustering_method_columns   = "ward.D2",
  na_col = "grey90",
  row_names_gp    = gpar(fontsize = 9),
  column_names_gp = gpar(fontsize = 8),
  column_title = "Food consumption by country (z-scores)"
)
```

Compare the row dendrogram with the scores plot you made earlier: the countries
fall into the same groups, even though the heatmap never saw a principal
component. Look at the block of dark red where Portugal, Italy and Spain meet
garlic and olive oil, and at the Nordic block on crisp bread and frozen foods.
The grey cells are the three missing values.

## Alternative Univariate Approaches

If multivariate methods don't provide sufficient clarity, what alternative approaches could you use?

### Quiz: Univariate alternatives

```{r quiz-univariate, echo=FALSE}
question("Which univariate approaches could you use here instead of PCA? (select all that apply)",
  answer("A one-way ANOVA per food item, comparing the geographic regions", correct = TRUE),
  answer("A t-test per food item when comparing just two groups of countries", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Correcting for multiple testing, because you run one test per food item", correct = TRUE),
  answer("Reporting whichever food has the largest PC1 loading, without any test"),
  type = "multiple",
  message = "Go variable by variable: a one-way ANOVA across the five regions, or a t-test if you reduce it to two groups (say Southern versus Northern). Because you would be running 20 tests - one per food - you must correct for multiple testing (Bonferroni, or Benjamini-Hochberg if you prefer to control the false discovery rate). What you lose compared with PCA is the correlation structure: univariate tests treat garlic and olive oil as two unrelated findings, whereas the loadings plot shows at a glance that they travel together."
)
```

### One-way ANOVA, food by food

The heatmap is suggestive but it is not a test. The univariate route is to take
each food in turn and ask whether the five regions differ, with a **one-way
ANOVA**. That means 20 separate tests, so we also correct the p-values for
multiple testing.

```{r anova-per-food, exercise=TRUE}
# One ANOVA per food: does consumption differ between the five regions?
region <- factor(food_data$Geographic_Location)

p_anova <- sapply(food_vars, function(food) {
  model <- aov(food_data[[food]] ~ region)
  summary(model)[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1]
})

anova_results <- data.frame(
  Food          = food_vars,
  p_raw         = round(p_anova, 4),
  p_BH          = round(p.adjust(p_anova, method = "BH"), 4),
  p_Bonferroni  = round(p.adjust(p_anova, method = "bonferroni"), 4)
)
anova_results <- anova_results[order(anova_results$p_raw), ]

head(anova_results, 8)

cat("\nFoods significant at 0.05:\n")
cat("  without correction:", sum(anova_results$p_raw < 0.05), "\n")
cat("  Benjamini-Hochberg:", sum(anova_results$p_BH < 0.05), "\n")
cat("  Bonferroni:        ", sum(anova_results$p_Bonferroni < 0.05), "\n")
```

```{r anova-per-food-solution}
region <- factor(food_data$Geographic_Location)
p_anova <- sapply(food_vars, function(food) {
  summary(aov(food_data[[food]] ~ region))[[1]][["Pr(>F)"]][1]
})
data.frame(Food = food_vars,
           p_raw = round(p_anova, 4),
           p_BH = round(p.adjust(p_anova, "BH"), 4),
           p_Bonferroni = round(p.adjust(p_anova, "bonferroni"), 4)) |>
  arrange(p_raw) |>
  head(8)
```

Look at what the correction does. Seven foods look significant if you ignore the
fact that you ran 20 tests; four survive Benjamini-Hochberg, and only **one** -
ground coffee - survives the strict Bonferroni correction. That is the price of
asking twenty questions of sixteen countries.

### t-test between two groups

If you narrow the question to two groups the test becomes a **t-test**. Compare
the Southern countries with the Northern ones, which is the contrast PC1
described:

```{r ttest-two-groups, exercise=TRUE}
# Keep only the Southern and Northern countries
two_groups <- food_data[food_data$Geographic_Location %in% c("S", "N"), ]

cat("Group sizes:\n")
print(table(two_groups$Geographic_Location))

p_ttest <- sapply(food_vars, function(food) {
  t.test(two_groups[[food]] ~ two_groups$Geographic_Location)$p.value
})

ttest_results <- data.frame(
  Food         = food_vars,
  p_raw        = round(p_ttest, 4),
  p_BH         = round(p.adjust(p_ttest, method = "BH"), 4),
  p_Bonferroni = round(p.adjust(p_ttest, method = "bonferroni"), 4)
)
ttest_results <- ttest_results[order(ttest_results$p_raw), ]

head(ttest_results, 8)
```

```{r ttest-two-groups-solution}
two_groups <- food_data[food_data$Geographic_Location %in% c("S", "N"), ]
p_ttest <- sapply(food_vars, function(food) {
  t.test(two_groups[[food]] ~ two_groups$Geographic_Location)$p.value
})
data.frame(Food = food_vars,
           p_raw = round(p_ttest, 4),
           p_BH = round(p.adjust(p_ttest, "BH"), 4),
           p_Bonferroni = round(p.adjust(p_ttest, "bonferroni"), 4)) |>
  arrange(p_raw) |>
  head(8)
```

Only two foods survive correction here: **garlic** and **olive oil** - exactly
the two the loadings plot pointed at. Note also how small the groups are (3
Southern and 4 Northern countries), which is why so little reaches significance.

Finally, plot the two winners so you can see what the p-values are describing:

```{r univariate-boxplot, exercise=TRUE, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
food_data |>
  select(Geographic_Location, Garlic, Olive_Oil) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Garlic, Olive_Oil),
               names_to = "Food", values_to = "Percentage") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Geographic_Location, y = Percentage,
             fill = Geographic_Location)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~Food) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = region_colors, labels = region_labels) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = region_labels) +
  labs(title = "The two foods that survive multiple-testing correction",
       x = NULL, y = "% of households", fill = "Region") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "none")
```

### Quiz: Alternative Univariate Approaches

```{r quiz-univariate-results, echo=FALSE}
quiz(
  question("The t-test finds garlic and olive oil, which is what the loadings plot already told you. So what did PCA add?",
    answer("PCA showed that garlic and olive oil vary *together*, and placed every country on one picture - twenty separate tests cannot do either", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Nothing - the two approaches are equivalent"),
    answer("PCA gave smaller p-values"),
    answer("PCA needed no assumptions about the data"),
    message = "The univariate tests hand you a ranked list of foods and nothing else: they treat garlic and olive oil as two unrelated findings, and they say nothing about which countries resemble which. PCA gives you the correlation structure and the map of countries in one go. Note also that PCA produces no p-values at all - the two approaches answer different questions, and in practice you want both."
  ),
  question("Why does the number of significant foods drop from 7 to 1 when you apply Bonferroni?",
    answer("Because running 20 tests at 0.05 would give about one false positive by chance alone, and Bonferroni protects against that very conservatively", correct = TRUE),
    answer("Because the ANOVA was calculated incorrectly"),
    answer("Because Bonferroni removes the missing values"),
    answer("Because there are only 16 countries"),
    message = "With 20 tests at a 0.05 threshold you expect 20 x 0.05 = 1 significant result purely by chance. Bonferroni divides the threshold by the number of tests (0.05/20 = 0.0025), which controls the chance of ANY false positive but throws away a lot of real signal. Benjamini-Hochberg is the middle road: it controls the *proportion* of false positives among your hits, and here it keeps four foods instead of one. Which you choose depends on whether a missed finding or a false one costs you more."
  )
)
```

## Summary and Key Takeaways

### What We've Learned

1. **Missing values need not stop you.** The NIPALS algorithm fits the model
   around the few empty cells, so nothing had to be removed or imputed first.
2. **Choose the number of components with Q², not R².** R² keeps rising with
   every component; Q² peaked around the third component and then fell. A low
   Q² (about 0.2 here) means the model is good for exploring, not for
   predicting - the broad patterns can still be real.
3. **Look beyond PC1 and PC2.** PC3 showed a pattern that the first two
   components hid (England and Ireland, with their low ground coffee).
4. **Read scores and loadings together, one component at a time.** Each
   component has two ends, and foods at one end are bought most in the
   countries at the same end of the scores plot.
5. **Check the raw data before you explain.** The obvious explanation is not
   always the right one: Portugal and England are separated mainly by tinned
   and processed foods, not by garlic and olive oil. In a biplot, a short arrow
   means a variable is poorly described in that plane, so do not read values
   from it.
6. **Extreme is not the same as an outlier.** Hotelling's T² and DModX tell you
   which samples to look at, not which ones to delete. With only 16
   observations the T² ellipse is very wide, so a small data set has little
   power to flag outliers at all.
7. **PCA and univariate tests answer different questions.** PCA shows which
   variables move together and maps all observations in one picture, but gives
   no p-values. Testing every variable separately does give p-values, but needs
   a correction for multiple testing and loses the correlation structure. A
   second unsupervised method, hierarchical clustering, found the same groups
   as the PCA.
